title: Dealing with ambiguity: context, probability, absurdity
summary: Japanese can look ambiguous, but three common-sense rules (context, probability and absurdity) settle almost every doubtful sentence.

blocks.text: Japanese has a name for being vague, and part of that is because of the **zero pronoun**: you cannot see the carriage. But the carriage is always there logically, and a hidden word works like English "it", which can mean anything and is only clear from context. Japanese is not magic. Speaker and listener fix doubts the same way English speakers do.
Three rules that settle most doubts

rows: What was said before points to the answer.
Talking about lunch, 私はうどんだ means "I'll have udon"
If two readings fit, take the likelier one.
私は猫を飼っている: you keep a cat, not a cat keeps you
Do not choose the silly reading unless the speaker makes the silliness clear.
私は魚だ means "I am the fish dish" at a restaurant, not that I am a fish

blocks.text: Speakers expect listeners to use these rules, and languages are built around that. A speaker who wants a strange meaning has to say so clearly. The stranger the meaning, the more the speaker has to explain.
A famous overlap: potential and receptive

The ichidan **potential** (食べられる, "can eat") and the ichidan **receptive** (食べられる, "receive being eaten") look the same. A single sentence 食べられた could mean either. Usually probability decides: nobody tells you "I got eaten" while standing there. With a pet mouse, however, ネズミが食べられた could be "the mouse could eat" or "the mouse got eaten", and only context can say. This kind of real ambiguity exists in English too.

A topic with は is not logical, but it still has to be **connected** to the comment after it. If a long sentence begins with 「あの人は」 and the comment has nothing to do with that person, the は-reading is unlikely. So the reader prefers a different structure.

blocks.jp: この果物は子供でも食べられる。
blocks.en: Even a child can eat this fruit. (potential; the situation makes that clear)

items: The zero pronoun is always there, and context says who or what it is.
Ichidan **-られる** can be potential or receptive; use the situation to decide.
A real ambiguity can exist, as in any language; the speaker is responsible for making things clear.

questions.instruction: Which three rules settle most doubtful sentences?
questions.note: These are common-sense rules for any language.

questions.instruction: At a restaurant a friend says 私はうなぎだ. What is the likeliest meaning?
questions.note: Context makes the food reading obvious.

questions.instruction: Which rule says that the silly reading needs clear signals from the speaker?
questions.note: The burden of making an absurd meaning clear is on the speaker.

questions.instruction: Which two meanings can 食べられた have?
options: Was able to eat / was eaten
questions.note: Potential and receptive share the form for ichidan verbs.

questions.prompt: In Japanese the carriage can be missing from the logical sentence entirely.
questions.note: It may be invisible (a zero), but it is always logically there.

questions.instruction: A speaker says 食べられた while standing there looking healthy. Which meaning wins?
questions.note: Probability: nobody who is standing there was eaten.

questions.instruction: ネズミが食べられた. What is needed to decide the meaning?
options: Context, such as a cat nearby or food given
questions.note: A real ambiguity is solved by the situation.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that carries both possible meanings
questions.note: 食べられた is the verb with the ambiguous helper られる.

questions.prompt: Such ambiguity is special to Japanese.
questions.note: English has famous cases too, such as seeing a man with a telescope.

questions.instruction: A は topic and its comment must be…
options: in the same clause as が
questions.note: A topic unrelated to its comment is an unlikely reading.

questions.instruction: Which invisible word is most probable in 「眠いから先に寝た」 said by a tired speaker?
questions.note: Context (眠い and 寝た) point back at the speaker.
